steps.user_message: I'm preparing my 2024 taxes and could use your help. Situation: married filing jointly, Phoenix AZ. W-2 from Metro Consulting: $88,100. Side income: $14,600 from data analysis (2 clients). Interest $1,780 (Synchrony Bank), dividends $550 (Interactive Brokers). Home office: 155 sq ft, rent $1,600/month, apartment 780 sq ft. Deductions: student loan interest $4,250 (Sallie Mae, 2019–2020); charity $2,000 to Local United Way have the receipt; unreimbursed expenses $720. Can you help me figure out deductions, standard vs itemized, and home office treatment—and which forms to use?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s a clear plan for your 2024 federal return based on what you shared. I’ll note assumptions and where a quick confirmation from you could change the numbers slightly.

Summary of what’s deductible for you
- Take the standard deduction (married filing jointly): $29,200 for 2024. Your itemizable amounts (e.g., $2,000 charity) are well below this, so itemizing wouldn’t help.
- Student loan interest: You paid $4,250, but the federal above‑the‑line deduction is capped at $2,500 (and your income is below the phase‑out), so you can deduct $2,500.
- Side business (data analysis) on Schedule C: Deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses, including a home office. If your “unreimbursed expenses” of $720 are for this side business, they belong on Schedule C and will reduce both income tax and self‑employment (SE) tax. If they’re for your W‑2 job, they are not deductible federally through 2025.
- Self‑employment tax: You’ll owe SE tax on your net profit; you also get an above‑the‑line deduction for half of it.
- QBI deduction: You should qualify for the 20% qualified business income deduction on your Schedule C profit (Form 8995), further reducing taxable income.

Home office deduction (exclusive and regular use required)
- Space: 155 sq ft in a 780 sq ft apartment = 19.9% business use.
- Rent: $1,600/month = $19,200/year.
- Two methods:
  1) Simplified: 155 sq ft × $5 = $775.
  2) Actual (recommended here): 19.9% × $19,200 rent ≈ $3,815. This yields a much larger deduction. It can’t create a Schedule C loss; any excess carries forward. As a renter, you won’t depreciate the home itself.
- You can also include a business share of utilities/renter’s insurance under the actual method if applicable (not provided yet).

Quick estimated 2024 federal results (assuming the $720 is NOT a business expense and using the actual home office)
- Income:
  - W‑2 wages: $88,100
  - Schedule C net profit (14,600 − 3,815 home office) ≈ $10,785
  - Interest: $1,780
  - Dividends: $550
  - Total income ≈ $101,215
- Adjustments:
  - Half SE tax ≈ $762
  - Student loan interest deduction: $2,500
  - Adjusted gross income (AGI) ≈ $97,953
- Deduction:
  - Standard deduction (MFJ): $29,200
  - Taxable income before QBI ≈ $68,753
  - QBI deduction ≈ 20% of (Schedule C profit minus half SE tax) ≈ 20% of ~$10,023 ≈ $2,005
  - Taxable income after QBI ≈ $66,748
- SE tax ≈ $1,524 (in addition to regular income tax)

If the $720 is a business expense on Schedule C
- Net profit would drop further, SE tax drops, AGI drops, and your QBI recalculates. Roughly, taxable income after QBI could fall by another ~$535 and SE tax by about ~$100 more—so it’s worth confirming.

Which forms to use
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1: Additional Income (business income flows from Schedule C) and Adjustments (student loan interest, half SE tax)
- Schedule B: You have >$1,500 of interest, so this is required for interest/dividends
- Schedule C: Side business income/expenses
- Schedule SE: Self‑employment tax
- Form 8829: Home office (if you use the actual expense method). If you choose the simplified method, you’ll use the Schedule C worksheet instead of Form 8829.
- Form 8995: Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction
- You’ll also need your year‑end tax docs: W‑2, 1099‑NEC(s) from clients (if issued), 1099‑INT (Synchrony), 1099‑DIV (IBKR), and 1098‑E (student loan interest)

A few quick confirmations to finalize
- Is the $720 of unreimbursed expenses related to your side data‑analysis work (Schedule C) or to your W‑2 job?
- Do you have any other side‑business expenses (software, supplies, phone/internet portion, mileage, etc.)?
- Any utilities or renter’s insurance we should include in the home office actual‑expense method?

If you’d like, I can draft a concise email to your CPA summarizing these figures and the open questions.
